summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old male with a history of type II diabetes, morbid obesity, atrial fibrillation, and prior right hallux amputation was admitted for a planned split-thickness skin graft from the right thigh to foot. Postoperatively, he developed worsening lower extremity edema and dyspnea, leading to transfer to the heart failure service for management of acute on chronic systolic heart failure. He was treated with intravenous and oral diuresis, achieving significant fluid loss and symptom improvement. His ejection fraction was found to be reduced at 35%, with moderate mitral regurgitation and pulmonary hypertension. The skin graft remained stable without infection. He was also managed for chronic blepharitis with ophthalmology input and optimized on heart failure and anticoagulation therapy. He was discharged home with follow-up arranged and instructions for weight monitoring, wound care, and medication adherence.
